Members of the US Secret Service detain a man near the scene of vehicle crash near Lafayette Square in Washington, DC, on November 9 [Pedro Ugarte/AFP]By ReutersPublished On 9 Nov 20269 Nov 2026
Two people have been detained near the White House following a pair of security breaches, according to the United States Secret Service agency (USSS).
One of the incidents, which occurred Monday morning, involved a suspect who drove a vehicle onto the pavement at Lafayette Park, which sits directly in front of the White House.
Recommended Stories list of 4 itemslist 1 of 4Trump orders DOJ to investigate Democrats for ‘threatening’ peoplelist 2 of 4US top Democrat backs impeachment of Pete Hegsethlist 3 of 4Qatar PM to meet Trump: What’s the latest on US-Iran negotiations?list 4 of 4Hackers target US campaign finance system days before midterm electionsend of list
Secret Service Police and National Guard units responded to reports of the vehicle crash at about 10am local time (15:00 GMT), according to a spokesperson for the federal law enforcement agency.
They converged on the northern edge of Lafayette Park near 16th and H Streets Northwest.
Around the same time, another suspect jumped a security barrier in the northwest corner of Lafayette Park. It is not clear if the two events were related.
President Donald Trump was inside the executive residence when the incidents occurred, prompting a brief White House lockdown and the closure of the surrounding roads.
The lockdown was lifted an hour later, according to the White House press pool.
Video footage of the incident captured a silver sedan emitting blankets of smoke as law enforcement officers surrounded it. It shows the driver exiting the vehicle and swinging at the gathered officers.

A co-founder of Al Jazeera's online services, political cartoonist Shujaat Ali has died aged 54 [File: Shujaat Ali via Facebook]By Al Jazeera StaffPublished On 9 Nov 20269 Nov 2026
Shujaat Ali, cartoonist and founding member of Al Jazeera’s online teams, has died at the age of 54.
A pioneer of digital cartoons, Ali was credited with creating the first animated caricatures online. He also worked at a number of media outlets in his native Pakistan and abroad, receiving several awards for his work.
Recommended Stories list of 2 itemslist 1 of 2Palestinian cartoonist sketches inspirationlist 2 of 2Drawing dangerously: Arab comics push the boundariesend of list
He died last week after suffering a heart attack as he returned home from work. He was buried in Qasimabad in Rawalpindi, where his parents are also buried.
Ali was Pakistan’s first court artist, documenting the course of a number of well-known cases using his pencil and skills.
He had recently been working with the Pakistan Air Force, his son-in-law, Waqar Saeed, told the Dawn newspaper.
Before returning to his homeland, he had worked at Al Jazeera for many years. He contributed as part of the founding team of Al Jazeera Arabic’s online services, developing cartooning to utilise the potential of the digital platform.
Ahmed El Amraoui, an editor at Aljazeera.com, said, “I had the privilege of working with Shujaat during the early days of Aljazeera.com. He was a very talented artist, but what made him stand out was how far ahead of his time he was.”Shujaat Ali received a number of national and international awards for his work as a cartoonist [File: Al Jazeera]

Fighters from the Saudi-led coalition hold a position during clashes with Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen's northwestern al-Jawf province on November 2, 2026 [File: AFP]By Mohammad MansourPublished On 9 Nov 20269 Nov 2026
Yemen’s government forces have announced the capture of Houthi-held positions in the southern governorate of Lahj, amid fierce clashes with the Houthi rebels across multiple fronts in the country.
The government’s National Shield Forces said on Monday that they had seized positions on the al-Muhawala front in western Lahj after a large-scale assault on Houthi positions. The forces claimed that dozens of Houthi fighters had been killed or wounded in the attack.

The latest announcement comes after several days of reported gains by government forces in the northern governorate of al-Jawf, east of the Houthi-held Yemeni capital Sanaa. Government forces in al-Jawf have advanced in recent days through mountain ranges east of the provincial capital al-Hazm.
Al Jazeera Arabic reporter Suhaib al-Miyahi visited the al-Jawf front line on November 6, documenting trenches and fortifications in positions that government commanders said had been captured from the Houthis, as battles continued nearby.
The Houthis are continuing their attacks in Taiz, where they have encircled the city, imposing a siege on it for more than a month. Government forces say they have repelled Houthi attacks across several fronts in the outskirts of the city over the previous day.

Journalists from Novaya Gazeta take part in a farewell action outside their editorial office in Moscow, November 9, 2026 [Maxim Shipenkov/EPA]By Al Jazeera Staff, AFP and ReutersPublished On 9 Nov 20269 Nov 2026
Russian investigative newspaper Novaya Gazeta has ended operations due to pressure from authorities.
The newspaper reported that it held its last editorial meeting on Monday and closed its newsroom. It announced last month that it was being forced to shut down after being classed as a “foreign agent” by Moscow, a label used to stifle dissent.
Recommended Stories list of 4 itemslist 1 of 4Why the Kremlin fears even the ‘managed opposition’ in Russialist 2 of 4Russia seizes assets of French firms, summons UK envoy over Ukraine supportlist 3 of 4Russia’s Novaya Gazeta ‘killed off’ after murders, arrests and pressurelist 4 of 4Russia ‘forces’ closure of investigative newspaper Novaya Gazetaend of list
The Russian media has come under increased scrutiny from the state amid Moscow’s war on Ukraine. In October, authorities searched the home of Novaya Gazeta’s editor-in-chief, Sergei Sokolov, and took him in for questioning. Another editor at the paper, Oleg Roldugin, was arrested in April.
Cofounder Dmitry Muratov addressed journalists who gathered to witness the closure of the Novaya Gazeta office in Moscow.
“Those in our country who advocate for peace have been denied the right to read what they choose, as we see happening today,” he said, adding that constitutional guarantees for political and civil rights had “effectively ceased to function”.
Novaya Gazeta was one of the few remaining outlets that openly criticised Russia’s war on Ukraine and the Kremlin’s policies, amid a widening crackdown on the media and free speech.

Meta will use AI to better identify teen users after agreeing to pay $18bn and boost protections of children on its platforms [File: Hollie Adams/Reuters]By Al Jazeera StaffPublished On 9 Nov 20269 Nov 2026
Social media giant Meta is expanding automated age-estimation technology globally starting this month following billion-dollar legal settlements and criticism that its platforms fail to protect teenagers from online harms.
“We use AI technology to find people we suspect to be teens, even if they use an adult birthday, and place them in Teen Account protections,” the company said in an announcement on Monday.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Landmark cases on social media’s impact on children begin this week in USlist 2 of 3Facebook found liable as TikTok settles for $100m over user safetylist 3 of 3Australia’s High Court hears bid to overturn under-16s social media banend of list
“Since first introducing this technology, we’ve been placing more teens in age-appropriate protections and are encouraged by the results. Based on that success, today we’re expanding this technology globally.”
Teen accounts have more restrictions and protections, limiting contacts, types of content and users’ time. Teens often circumvent the restrictions by creating a fake birthday when they set up an account, raising concerns that minors could bypass parental controls and be exposed to harmful content.
Parents in the United States who have set up Instagram for teenagers will receive notifications this month about the new measures. Meta said it will expand the age estimation algorithm to Facebook and Threads later in the year.

Demonstrators march towards Place de la Nation in Paris during a protest over the cost of living crisis organised by a coalition of student groups and trade unions [File: Elke Scholiers/Getty Images]By Al Jazeera Staff, AFP and ReutersPublished On 9 Nov 20269 Nov 2026
The French government has announced it will move a planned rise in the minimum wage forward by a month as it seeks to quell mass protests over the cost of living.
French ⁠Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu announced on Monday that the 1.6 percent increase in the minimum wage, originally planned for the start of 2027, will now take effect from December 1, 2026.
Recommended Stories list of 4 itemslist 1 of 4Radical or hero?: France debates leftist candidate Jean-Luc Melenchonlist 2 of 4Protesters break into Microsoft data centre site in Amsterdamlist 3 of 4More than 140,000 rally as new protests against rising costs sweep Francelist 4 of 4Mapping how France’s protest wave spread across Europeend of list
The move comes amid weeks of student-led demonstrations that started with calls for greater investment for the country’s underfunded schools but have morphed into broader protests and serious unrest – part of a wave across Europe.
The minimum monthly wage in France currently stands at 1,477.93 euros ($1,656); the increase raises it by 24 euros ($27) to 1,502 euros ($1,683).
“Regarding the SMIC [minimum wage], we have decided two things: to bring forward the increase to 1 December as opposed to 1 January, and to raise this increase to 1.6 per cent,” said Labour Minister Jean-Pierre Farandou at a press conference.
This increase represents “the second-largest rise in 20 years; it should not be underestimated”, Lecornu told reporters, stressing that this boost is “not merely symbolic”.
